content: Vitamin D is universally recommended to prevent vitamin D deficiency. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) guidelines suggest a daily intake of 600 IU for healthy individuals aged 1 to 70 years and 800 IU for those over 70 years of age. Primary prevention of vitamin D deficiency involves dietary intake and cutaneous synthesis. Cutaneous synthesis requires adequate sun exposure, which is influenced by factors such as season, latitude, altitude, duration of exposure, and skin pigmentation. However, concerns about increased skin cancer risk from sun exposure mean that sun exposure is not recommended as a primary method to prevent vitamin D deficiency. In 2011, the IOM recommended a daily intake of 600 IU of vitamin D for healthy individuals over the age of 1 until 70 years. For individuals over 70 years of age, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is 800 IU per day. Pregnant and lactating women are advised to follow the same RDA as non-pregnant adults. The National Osteoporosis Foundation (NOF) recommends a higher dose of 800–1000 IU of vitamin D daily for adults aged 50 years and older. In the United Kingdom, the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN) recommends a daily intake of 400 IU (10 micrograms) of vitamin D for everyone over the age of one year.
